cooling_items.text:
The building is not equipped with a centralized cooling system. Cooling within individual suites is provided by a combination of window-mounted air conditioners and portable indoor air-conditioning units.

These decentralized cooling devices are generally less efficient than modern centralized or heat-pump-based systems. Typical window and portable air-conditioning units operate with relatively low coefficients of performance (COP), often below 3.0, compared to high-efficiency heat pump systems which can achieve COP values exceeding 4.5–5.0 under favorable conditions.

In addition to reduced cooling efficiency, window-mounted air-conditioning units can negatively impact building envelope performance. Improper sealing around window installations may allow uncontrolled air infiltration during the heating season, increasing heat loss, draft complaints, and overall space-heating energy consumption. Installation of a air source heat pump (ASHP) system could be considered in a short term to mid term.

measures.existing_conditions: The building’s HVAC systems operate using a mixture of local controls and a legacy building automation system (BAS) that provides limited monitoring capability. The control platform has not been comprehensively updated or recalibrated for several years, and the level of integration varies across equipment. Many components operate with minimal feedback, limited scheduling capability, and reduced visibility into equipment performance. Legacy or partially obsolete control devices are difficult to maintain, prone to failures, and may no longer be fully supported by the manufacturer.
measures.notes: Modernise the existing BAS and field devices onto an open digital platform with full feedback, trending and alarms to improve reliability, visibility and HVAC optimisation opportunities.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommends implementing a comprehensive BAS upgrade to provide modern, centralized control and monitoring of all major HVAC systems. The retrofit would consolidate the existing control infrastructure into a unified digital platform capable of advanced sequencing, optimized scheduling, remote monitoring, trending, and alarms. Outdated control devices would be replaced with new DDC components. A non-proprietary framework such as Niagara 4 is recommended to allow future expansion and easier maintenance. The upgraded BAS is expected to reduce energy use, improve comfort, and extend equipment service life. Enbridge Gas incentive programs for advanced building controls can help offset capital costs and improve project payback.

*Where applicable, IESO incentives and Enbridge incentives for central heating system efficiency upgrades may be available and could help improve overall project economics. Additional information regarding current incentive programs can be found on Mann Engineering’s website:
https://www.mannengineering.com/100-000-enbridge-incentive

measures.existing_conditions:
The existing heating boilers in the mechanical room are non-condensing, gas-fired {______ }units installed in {______}, with an estimated thermal efficiency of approximately {_______}%. As non-condensing equipment, they operate with higher flue-gas temperatures and cannot recover latent heat from combustion, resulting in reduced overall efficiency compared to modern condensing boiler technologies.

The boilers also {not integrate with BAS}, lack advanced control features such as setpoint adjustment based on outdoor air temperature and real-time modulation optimization. This limited control capability contributes to frequent short cycling and increased natural gas consumption. As a result, the system experiences elevated utility costs and higher greenhouse gas emissions.

While the boilers remain operational and continue to provide reliable heating performance, their age and conventional atmospheric design limit overall system efficiency compared to modern condensing technology. Although there is no immediate need for replacement, planning for a long-term boiler upgrade would allow the building to benefit from improved energy efficiency, reduced operating costs, and enhanced modulation and control capabilities in future years.
measures.notes: Replace aging non condensing boilers with high-efficiency condensing units and improved piping to enable true condensing operation, lowering gas consumption improve overall energy efficiency and extending plant life.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommended that the existing non-condensing boilers be replaced with high-efficiency condensing boilers. Condensing boilers are designed to extract additional heat from the flue gases by recovering latent heat through a secondary heat exchanger, allowing them to achieve thermal efficiencies of up to 98%. This upgrade would substantially reduce natural gas consumption, lower utility costs, and improve overall system performance.

Modern condensing boilers also provide advanced control capabilities, including high-turndown modulation, integrated sequencing, and seamless compatibility with Building Automation Systems (BAS). These features improve load matching, reduce equipment cycling, and enhance operational reliability.

Upgrading to condensing boiler technology not only increases energy efficiency and reduces ongoing operating costs but also supports long-term sustainability objectives and contributes to meaningful reductions in greenhouse gas emissions. Piping would be reconfigured to reduce standby losses and protect the boilers from thermal shock.

measures.existing_conditions:
The domestic hot water (DHW) system is served by an indirect storage tank connected to the central boiler plant. The storage tank, associated DHW circulation pumps, and portions of the DHW piping were observed to be original to the building and approaching the end of their expected service life. 
In addition, two (2) atmospheric LAARS gas-fired DHW boilers, installed in 2003 with an estimated thermal efficiency of approximately 78%, are approaching the end of their expected service life. As atmospheric boilers, these units operate without condensing capability and therefore at lower thermal efficiency compared to modern condensing DHW boiler systems.
Aging indirect storage tanks typically require periodic internal relining and increased maintenance effort to maintain performance and water quality. As these components continue to age, maintenance requirements, the risk of unplanned service interruptions, and lifecycle costs are expected to increase.
measures.measure_title: Replace Aging DHW Storage Tank and piping and Condensing DHW Boiler Retrofit
measures.notes: Replace aging indirect DHW storage tanks and atmospheric DHW boilers with glass-lined storage tanks and high-efficiency condensing DHW boilers to increase boiler efficiency, reduce maintenance requirements.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
As part of the boiler plant and hydronic system reconfiguration, Mann recommends upgrading the DHW system through a comprehensive DHW modernization approach, including:
•	Replacement of the existing aging indirect storage tank with new vertical glass-lined DHW storage tanks; 
•	Replacement of the existing atmospheric DHW boilers with high-efficiency condensing DHW boilers, capable of achieving thermal efficiencies of up to approximately 98% under suitable operating conditions.
Under the proposed configuration, the condensing DHW boilers would directly serve the new glass-lined storage tanks. Upgrading to condensing boiler technology allows the system to operate at lower return-water temperatures, enabling latent heat recovery and significantly improving overall thermal efficiency.

The new storage tanks provide improved durability, reduced internal maintenance requirements, and more stable domestic hot water temperature control compared to aging indirect tanks.

Together, these upgrades reduce long-term maintenance requirements, improve system reliability, lower natural gas consumption.

measures.existing_conditions: The existing piping arrangement separates the space-heating and domestic hot water (DHW) systems into independent loops. The space-heating system operates with a primary distribution loop serving building loads, while the DHW system is served by a dedicated boiler loop with separate circulation. This configuration can limit system-level temperature coordination between heating and DHW loads and may contribute to inefficient boiler operation during part-load or shoulder-season conditions.
measures.measure_title: Primary–Secondary Boiler and DHW Piping Reconfiguration
measures.notes: Reconfigure heating and DHW piping to a primary–secondary layout, hydraulically separating loops to improve temperature control, boiler protection and plant efficiency.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
It is recommended to reconfigure the heating and DHW piping into a Primary–Secondary (P-S) hydronic arrangement. In a P-S design, the boiler primary loop circulates hot water while secondary loops draw only the flow required for each load, including space heating zones and DHW generation.

This configuration provides hydraulic separation between the boiler plant and building loads, improves system stability during varying load conditions, and enables more effective outdoor-air temperature reset strategies and control optimization.

With improved hydraulic separation, future system upgrades such as enhanced DHW generation strategies or alternative DHW configurations may also become feasible. When combined with a condensing boiler retrofit, the boiler plant may potentially be optimized in size and staging strategy, reducing capital and long-term maintenance costs.. Further engineering review is required to finalize the detailed design.

measures.existing_conditions:
The building is currently served by a heating-only hydronic distribution system. Space heating is provided through copper-fin baseboard heaters and hydronic radiators supplied by a centralized boiler plant located in the main mechanical room.

The building does not have a central cooling system. No in-suite fan coil units, chillers, or centralized cooling infrastructure are present. As a result, suite-level cooling, where provided, relies on window A/C or portable air-conditioning units. These localized cooling devices typically operate independently, are relatively inefficient, and contribute to increased electrical demand during the cooling season.
measures.measure_title: Convert Baseboard Heater to Mini-Split Heat Pump Systems
measures.notes: Replace current system with air-source heat pumps, allowing simultaneous heating and cooling.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommends replacing the existing hydronic baseboard heating systems with mini-split air-source heat pump (ASHP) systems to provide both space heating and cooling at the suite level.

The existing hydronic baseboard system relies on centrally generated hot water distributed throughout the building. While functional for heating, this system provides heating only, operates at relatively high distribution temperatures, and does not provide cooling. In addition, system efficiency is constrained by boiler plant performance, distribution losses, and limited zone-level control.

In contrast, mini-split heat pump systems typically operate at a COP of approximately 3 to 4 under suitable operating conditions, allowing them to deliver three to four units of heat for each unit of electrical energy consumed by transferring heat from the outdoor air to the indoor space. This results in a substantial reduction in energy consumption while maintaining or improving occupant comfort.

In addition to improved heating efficiency, the proposed mini-split systems would introduce dedicated cooling capability to the suites. This would eliminate the need for separate window-mounted or portable air-conditioning units, improving overall system efficiency, reducing peak electrical demand, and simplifying long-term maintenance.

The proposed upgrade would transition the building from an aging, single-function heating system to a modern, high-efficiency heating and cooling solution, improving occupant comfort, operational performance, and long-term energy efficiency.

*This measure is recommended subject to a detailed feasibility study to be carried out at the next project stage or as part of an ASHRAE Level 2 Energy Audit. The feasibility assessment should consider the available electrical service capacity, potential electrical infrastructure upgrades, and system integration constraints. It is also recommended that the existing hydronic heating system be retained as a backup system to ensure reliability and operational flexibility.

measures.existing_conditions: The building is served by gas-fired DX rooftop MUA units that provide tempered fresh air to corridors. Units have limited modulation capability, appear to operate at constant or manually set speeds, and are not fully integrated with the BAS. Burners, DX sections, and controls are aging, and continuous or high airflow during mild weather contributes to excessive gas and electrical consumption.
measures.measure_title: MUA Hydronic Conversion with BAS and VFDs
measures.notes: Convert DX gas MUAs to hydronic coils with VFD fans and full BAS control, combining high-efficiency central heating with demand-based ventilation and fan turndown.
measures.retrofit_conditions: It is recommended to convert the DX gas-fired MUAs to hydronic heating served by the central boiler plant, add VFDs on supply fans where feasible, and fully integrate the units with the BAS. New hydronic coils, modulating dampers, fan-speed control, and supply-air temperature reset will allow demand-based ventilation and improved corridor pressurization. Transferring heating to a high-efficiency condensing boiler plant will reduce gas use, while VFDs lower fan energy and mechanical wear. BAS integration will enable optimized scheduling, monitoring, and alarms. Enbridge incentives for central heating and control upgrades can help improve project payback.

measures.existing_conditions: No anti-scale thermostatic mixing valve was observed downstream of the domestic hot water storage tank during the site visit.As a result, delivery temperatures are controlled locally or through fixed settings, increasing the risk of temperature fluctuation, scalding, and scale buildup within downstream piping and fixtures.
measures.notes: Install an anti-scale thermostatic mixing valve to improve DHW temperature control, enhance occupant safety, and reduce scaling-related maintenance.
measures.retrofit_conditions: Install an anti-scale thermostatic mixing valve on the domestic hot water system to maintain safe and stable delivery temperatures while protecting downstream piping and fixtures from scale buildup. This measure improves temperature control, reduces scald risk, and lowers long-term maintenance requirements by minimizing mineral scaling within the DHW system.

measures.existing_conditions: The {domestic hot water (DHW) system} and {make-up air (MUA) heating coils} are currently served by shell-and-tube heat exchangers connected to the primary heating loop. While these heat exchangers remain operational, shell-and-tube units typically require more space and are generally more difficult to service due to their construction. Maintenance activities such as inspection, descaling, and cleaning can be labor-intensive, which may limit long-term maintainability. In addition, shell-and-tube heat exchangers generally operate with lower heat transfer efficiency compared to modern plate-type heat exchangers.
measures.measure_title: Replace Shell-and-Tube Heat Exchangers with Plate-and-Frame Heat Exchangers {DHW and MUA Systems}
measures.notes: Replacing the existing shell-and-tube heat exchangers with modern plate-and-frame heat exchangers would improve heat transfer efficiency and significantly simplify long-term maintenance of systems.
measures.retrofit_conditions: It is recommended to replace the existing shell-and-tube heat exchangers serving the {DHW} and {MUA} systems with high-efficiency plate-and-frame heat exchangers. Plate-and-frame units provide higher heat transfer efficiency and allow closer temperature approaches between the primary and secondary loops. Their modular plate construction allows the exchanger to be easily opened for inspection, cleaning, and maintenance, significantly improving serviceability. This retrofit would improve overall heat transfer performance, simplify maintenance procedures, and enhance the long-term reliability and operational efficiency of both the DHW and ventilation heating systems.

measures.existing_conditions: Domestic cold water is currently pressurized by a constant-speed booster pump with a downstream pressure-reducing or regulating valve to maintain setpoint pressure. The valve introduces unnecessary head loss and wastes pumping energy, and the pump operates at full speed even when demand is low.
measures.notes: Convert the constant-speed domestic booster pump to VFD control, eliminating throttling losses and matching pressure to demand for significant pump-energy savings.
measures.retrofit_conditions: It is recommended to install a variable frequency drive (VFD) on the domestic water booster pump and remove or bypass the pressure regulating valve. The VFD will control pump speed to maintain the desired discharge pressure directly, allowing the pump to slow down during periods of low demand. This reduces energy use, pump wear and noise while maintaining adequate system pressure. Further engineering is required to confirm setpoints, sensor locations and control logic.

measures.existing_conditions: The building is equipped with double-pane windows typical of its construction era. The windows were observed to be in generally fair condition at the time of the site visit. However, in aging buildings, the insulating glazing units (IGUs) may gradually lose performance over time due to seal deterioration and potential reduction of the insulating gas between panes. While no widespread failure was observed, long-term thermal performance may decline as glazing systems age.
measures.measure_title: Window Lifecycle Planning and Sealant Renewal (Aging Double-Glazed Units)
measures.notes: Monitor aging double-pane windows and incorporate sealant renewal and long-term glazing upgrades into lifecycle and capital planning strategies.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
As part of ongoing building envelope maintenance and long-term capital planning, it is recommended to monitor window performance and implement periodic re-caulking and weatherstripping renewal where required. Full window replacement is not considered immediately necessary; however, future glazing upgrades should be evaluated in alignment with reserve fund studies and envelope lifecycle planning. Proactive lifecycle management will help maintain thermal performance, occupant comfort, and overall energy efficiency over time.

New glazing systems with improved low-E coatings, warm-edge spacers, and enhanced seal performance would significantly reduce heat loss, improve occupant comfort, and lower heating demand. Phased implementation can be considered to align with reserve fund planning and envelope lifecycle scheduling.

measures.existing_conditions: Several mechanical and electrical systems in the building rely on routine maintenance to maintain efficiency, but many components have not been proactively upgraded or recommissioned. Heat exchangers may have scale or fouling, older motors may be standard-efficiency models, and controls or thermostats may be outdated or non-programmable.
measures.notes: Implement a bundle of low-cost maintenance upgrades—cleaning heat exchangers, replacing old motors, improving appliances and thermostats—to recover lost efficiency and reduce failures.
measures.retrofit_conditions: It is recommended to implement a package of miscellaneous maintenance and upgrade items. Typical measures include cleaning and descaling heat exchangers, replacing failed or obsolete motors with high-efficiency models, maintaining combustion air paths, upgrading in-suite appliances to ENERGY STAR models as they fail, and replacing non-programmable thermostats with programmable or smart thermostats. These actions reduce long-term maintenance costs, improve system efficiency and extend equipment life with relatively low capital investment.

measures.existing_conditions: At the present, the building relies on external utilities to provide electricity to power the building which might lead to high electrical energy costs.
measures.notes: Install net metered solar PV generated electricity to offset electricity consumption.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
The current state of the solar industry in Ontario is focused on “net metering” as power export to the grid is no longer an option. Rather than power export, net metered solar facilities use the generated electricity to offset electricity consumption within the facility. Since power export is not feasible, the system should be sized to only meet the baseload energy consumption of the building. This building has a high electrical consumption and ample roof space, which makes it a candidate for solar PV. 

A preliminary study is required to accurately estimate the system cost and savings for a Solar PV system

measures.existing_conditions: The building’s HVAC systems operate using a mixture of local controls and a legacy building automation system (BAS) that provides limited monitoring capability. The control platform has not been comprehensively updated or recalibrated for several years, and the level of integration varies across equipment. Many components operate with minimal feedback, limited scheduling capability, and reduced visibility into equipment performance. Legacy or partially obsolete control devices are difficult to maintain, prone to failures, and may no longer be fully supported by the manufacturer.
measures.notes: Modernise the existing BAS and field devices onto an open digital platform with full feedback, trending and alarms to improve reliability, visibility and HVAC optimisation opportunities.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommends implementing a comprehensive BAS upgrade to provide modern, centralized control and monitoring of all major HVAC systems. The retrofit would consolidate the existing control infrastructure into a unified digital platform capable of advanced sequencing, optimized scheduling, remote monitoring, trending, and alarms. Outdated control devices would be replaced with new DDC components. A non-proprietary framework such as Niagara 4 is recommended to allow future expansion and easier maintenance. The upgraded BAS is expected to reduce energy use, improve comfort, and extend equipment service life. Enbridge Gas incentive programs for advanced building controls can help offset capital costs and improve project payback.

*Where applicable, IESO incentives and Enbridge incentives for central heating system efficiency upgrades may be available and could help improve overall project economics. Additional information regarding current incentive programs can be found on Mann Engineering’s website:
https://www.mannengineering.com/100-000-enbridge-incentive

The existing heating boilers in the mechanical room are non-condensing, gas-fired {______ }units installed in {______}, with an estimated thermal efficiency of approximately {_______}%. As non-condensing equipment, they operate with higher flue-gas temperatures and cannot recover latent heat from combustion, resulting in reduced overall efficiency compared to modern condensing boiler technologies.

The boilers also {not integrate with BAS}, lack advanced control features such as setpoint adjustment based on outdoor air temperature and real-time modulation optimization. This limited control capability contributes to frequent short cycling and increased natural gas consumption. As a result, the system experiences elevated utility costs and higher greenhouse gas emissions.

While the boilers remain operational and continue to provide reliable heating performance, their age and conventional atmospheric design limit overall system efficiency compared to modern condensing technology. Although there is no immediate need for replacement, planning for a long-term boiler upgrade would allow the building to benefit from improved energy efficiency, reduced operating costs, and enhanced modulation and control capabilities in future years.
measures.notes: Replace aging non condensing boilers with high-efficiency condensing units and improved piping to enable true condensing operation, lowering gas consumption improve overall energy efficiency and extending plant life.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommended that the existing non-condensing boilers be replaced with high-efficiency condensing boilers. Condensing boilers are designed to extract additional heat from the flue gases by recovering latent heat through a secondary heat exchanger, allowing them to achieve thermal efficiencies of up to 98%. This upgrade would substantially reduce natural gas consumption, lower utility costs, and improve overall system performance.

Modern condensing boilers also provide advanced control capabilities, including high-turndown modulation, integrated sequencing, and seamless compatibility with Building Automation Systems (BAS). These features improve load matching, reduce equipment cycling, and enhance operational reliability.

Upgrading to condensing boiler technology not only increases energy efficiency and reduces ongoing operating costs but also supports long-term sustainability objectives and contributes to meaningful reductions in greenhouse gas emissions. Piping would be reconfigured to reduce standby losses and protect the boilers from thermal shock.

measures.existing_conditions:
The domestic hot water (DHW) system is served by an indirect storage tank connected to the central boiler plant. The storage tank, associated DHW circulation pumps, and portions of the DHW piping were observed to be original to the building and approaching the end of their expected service life. 
In addition, two (2) atmospheric LAARS gas-fired DHW boilers, installed in 2003 with an estimated thermal efficiency of approximately 78%, are approaching the end of their expected service life. As atmospheric boilers, these units operate without condensing capability and therefore at lower thermal efficiency compared to modern condensing DHW boiler systems.
Aging indirect storage tanks typically require periodic internal relining and increased maintenance effort to maintain performance and water quality. As these components continue to age, maintenance requirements, the risk of unplanned service interruptions, and lifecycle costs are expected to increase.
measures.measure_title: Replace Aging DHW Storage Tank and piping and Condensing DHW Boiler Retrofit
measures.notes: Replace aging indirect DHW storage tanks and atmospheric DHW boilers with glass-lined storage tanks and high-efficiency condensing DHW boilers to increase boiler efficiency, reduce maintenance requirements.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
As part of the boiler plant and hydronic system reconfiguration, Mann recommends upgrading the DHW system through a comprehensive DHW modernization approach, including:
•	Replacement of the existing aging indirect storage tank with new vertical glass-lined DHW storage tanks; 
•	Replacement of the existing atmospheric DHW boilers with high-efficiency condensing DHW boilers, capable of achieving thermal efficiencies of up to approximately 98% under suitable operating conditions.
Under the proposed configuration, the condensing DHW boilers would directly serve the new glass-lined storage tanks. Upgrading to condensing boiler technology allows the system to operate at lower return-water temperatures, enabling latent heat recovery and significantly improving overall thermal efficiency.

The new storage tanks provide improved durability, reduced internal maintenance requirements, and more stable domestic hot water temperature control compared to aging indirect tanks.

Together, these upgrades reduce long-term maintenance requirements, improve system reliability, lower natural gas consumption.

measures.existing_conditions: The existing piping arrangement separates the space-heating and domestic hot water (DHW) systems into independent loops. The space-heating system operates with a primary distribution loop serving building loads, while the DHW system is served by a dedicated boiler loop with separate circulation. This configuration can limit system-level temperature coordination between heating and DHW loads and may contribute to inefficient boiler operation during part-load or shoulder-season conditions.
measures.measure_title: Primary–Secondary Boiler and DHW Piping Reconfiguration
measures.notes: Reconfigure heating and DHW piping to a primary–secondary layout, hydraulically separating loops to improve temperature control, boiler protection and plant efficiency.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
It is recommended to reconfigure the heating and DHW piping into a Primary–Secondary (P-S) hydronic arrangement. In a P-S design, the boiler primary loop circulates hot water while secondary loops draw only the flow required for each load, including space heating zones and DHW generation.

This configuration provides hydraulic separation between the boiler plant and building loads, improves system stability during varying load conditions, and enables more effective outdoor-air temperature reset strategies and control optimization.

With improved hydraulic separation, future system upgrades such as enhanced DHW generation strategies or alternative DHW configurations may also become feasible. When combined with a condensing boiler retrofit, the boiler plant may potentially be optimized in size and staging strategy, reducing capital and long-term maintenance costs.. Further engineering review is required to finalize the detailed design.

measures.existing_conditions:
The building is currently served by a heating-only hydronic distribution system. Space heating is provided through copper-fin baseboard heaters and hydronic radiators supplied by a centralized boiler plant located in the main mechanical room.

The building does not have a central cooling system. No in-suite fan coil units, chillers, or centralized cooling infrastructure are present. As a result, suite-level cooling, where provided, relies on window A/C or portable air-conditioning units. These localized cooling devices typically operate independently, are relatively inefficient, and contribute to increased electrical demand during the cooling season.
measures.measure_title: Convert Baseboard Heater to Mini-Split Heat Pump Systems
measures.notes: Replace current system with air-source heat pumps, allowing simultaneous heating and cooling.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommends replacing the existing hydronic baseboard heating systems with mini-split air-source heat pump (ASHP) systems to provide both space heating and cooling at the suite level.

The existing hydronic baseboard system relies on centrally generated hot water distributed throughout the building. While functional for heating, this system provides heating only, operates at relatively high distribution temperatures, and does not provide cooling. In addition, system efficiency is constrained by boiler plant performance, distribution losses, and limited zone-level control.

In contrast, mini-split heat pump systems typically operate at a COP of approximately 3 to 4 under suitable operating conditions, allowing them to deliver three to four units of heat for each unit of electrical energy consumed by transferring heat from the outdoor air to the indoor space. This results in a substantial reduction in energy consumption while maintaining or improving occupant comfort.

In addition to improved heating efficiency, the proposed mini-split systems would introduce dedicated cooling capability to the suites. This would eliminate the need for separate window-mounted or portable air-conditioning units, improving overall system efficiency, reducing peak electrical demand, and simplifying long-term maintenance.

The proposed upgrade would transition the building from an aging, single-function heating system to a modern, high-efficiency heating and cooling solution, improving occupant comfort, operational performance, and long-term energy efficiency.

*This measure is recommended subject to a detailed feasibility study to be carried out at the next project stage or as part of an ASHRAE Level 2 Energy Audit. The feasibility assessment should consider the available electrical service capacity, potential electrical infrastructure upgrades, and system integration constraints. It is also recommended that the existing hydronic heating system be retained as a backup system to ensure reliability and operational flexibility.

*Where applicable, IESO incentives and Enbridge incentives for central heating system efficiency upgrades may be available and could help improve overall project economics. Additional information regarding current incentive programs can be found on Mann Engineering’s website:
https://www.mannengineering.com/100-000-enbridge-incentive

measures.existing_conditions: The building is served by gas-fired DX rooftop MUA units that provide tempered fresh air to corridors. Units have limited modulation capability, appear to operate at constant or manually set speeds, and are not fully integrated with the BAS. Burners, DX sections, and controls are aging, and continuous or high airflow during mild weather contributes to excessive gas and electrical consumption.
measures.measure_title: MUA Hydronic Conversion with BAS and VFDs
measures.notes: Convert DX gas MUAs to hydronic coils with VFD fans and full BAS control, combining high-efficiency central heating with demand-based ventilation and fan turndown.
measures.retrofit_conditions: It is recommended to convert the DX gas-fired MUAs to hydronic heating served by the central boiler plant, add VFDs on supply fans where feasible, and fully integrate the units with the BAS. New hydronic coils, modulating dampers, fan-speed control, and supply-air temperature reset will allow demand-based ventilation and improved corridor pressurization. Transferring heating to a high-efficiency condensing boiler plant will reduce gas use, while VFDs lower fan energy and mechanical wear. BAS integration will enable optimized scheduling, monitoring, and alarms. Enbridge incentives for central heating and control upgrades can help improve project payback.

measures.existing_conditions: No anti-scale thermostatic mixing valve was observed downstream of the domestic hot water storage tank during the site visit.As a result, delivery temperatures are controlled locally or through fixed settings, increasing the risk of temperature fluctuation, scalding, and scale buildup within downstream piping and fixtures.
measures.notes: Install an anti-scale thermostatic mixing valve to improve DHW temperature control, enhance occupant safety, and reduce scaling-related maintenance.
measures.retrofit_conditions: Install an anti-scale thermostatic mixing valve on the domestic hot water system to maintain safe and stable delivery temperatures while protecting downstream piping and fixtures from scale buildup. This measure improves temperature control, reduces scald risk, and lowers long-term maintenance requirements by minimizing mineral scaling within the DHW system.

measures.existing_conditions: The {domestic hot water (DHW) system} and {make-up air (MUA) heating coils} are currently served by shell-and-tube heat exchangers connected to the primary heating loop. While these heat exchangers remain operational, shell-and-tube units typically require more space and are generally more difficult to service due to their construction. Maintenance activities such as inspection, descaling, and cleaning can be labor-intensive, which may limit long-term maintainability. In addition, shell-and-tube heat exchangers generally operate with lower heat transfer efficiency compared to modern plate-type heat exchangers.
measures.measure_title: Replace Shell-and-Tube Heat Exchangers with Plate-and-Frame Heat Exchangers {DHW and MUA Systems}
measures.notes: Replacing the existing shell-and-tube heat exchangers with modern plate-and-frame heat exchangers would improve heat transfer efficiency and significantly simplify long-term maintenance of systems.
measures.retrofit_conditions: It is recommended to replace the existing shell-and-tube heat exchangers serving the {DHW} and {MUA} systems with high-efficiency plate-and-frame heat exchangers. Plate-and-frame units provide higher heat transfer efficiency and allow closer temperature approaches between the primary and secondary loops. Their modular plate construction allows the exchanger to be easily opened for inspection, cleaning, and maintenance, significantly improving serviceability. This retrofit would improve overall heat transfer performance, simplify maintenance procedures, and enhance the long-term reliability and operational efficiency of both the DHW and ventilation heating systems.

measures.existing_conditions: Domestic cold water is currently pressurized by a constant-speed booster pump with a downstream pressure-reducing or regulating valve to maintain setpoint pressure. The valve introduces unnecessary head loss and wastes pumping energy, and the pump operates at full speed even when demand is low.
measures.notes: Convert the constant-speed domestic booster pump to VFD control, eliminating throttling losses and matching pressure to demand for significant pump-energy savings.
measures.retrofit_conditions: It is recommended to install a variable frequency drive (VFD) on the domestic water booster pump and remove or bypass the pressure regulating valve. The VFD will control pump speed to maintain the desired discharge pressure directly, allowing the pump to slow down during periods of low demand. This reduces energy use, pump wear and noise while maintaining adequate system pressure. Further engineering is required to confirm setpoints, sensor locations and control logic.

measures.existing_conditions: The building is equipped with double-pane windows typical of its construction era. The windows were observed to be in generally fair condition at the time of the site visit. However, in aging buildings, the insulating glazing units (IGUs) may gradually lose performance over time due to seal deterioration and potential reduction of the insulating gas between panes. While no widespread failure was observed, long-term thermal performance may decline as glazing systems age.
measures.measure_title: Window Lifecycle Planning and Sealant Renewal (Aging Double-Glazed Units)
measures.notes: Monitor aging double-pane windows and incorporate sealant renewal and long-term glazing upgrades into lifecycle and capital planning strategies.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
As part of ongoing building envelope maintenance and long-term capital planning, it is recommended to monitor window performance and implement periodic re-caulking and weatherstripping renewal where required. Full window replacement is not considered immediately necessary; however, future glazing upgrades should be evaluated in alignment with reserve fund studies and envelope lifecycle planning. Proactive lifecycle management will help maintain thermal performance, occupant comfort, and overall energy efficiency over time.

New glazing systems with improved low-E coatings, warm-edge spacers, and enhanced seal performance would significantly reduce heat loss, improve occupant comfort, and lower heating demand. Phased implementation can be considered to align with reserve fund planning and envelope lifecycle scheduling.

measures.existing_conditions: Several mechanical and electrical systems in the building rely on routine maintenance to maintain efficiency, but many components have not been proactively upgraded or recommissioned. Heat exchangers may have scale or fouling, older motors may be standard-efficiency models, and controls or thermostats may be outdated or non-programmable.
measures.notes: Implement a bundle of low-cost maintenance upgrades—cleaning heat exchangers, replacing old motors, improving appliances and thermostats—to recover lost efficiency and reduce failures.
measures.retrofit_conditions: It is recommended to implement a package of miscellaneous maintenance and upgrade items. Typical measures include cleaning and descaling heat exchangers, replacing failed or obsolete motors with high-efficiency models, maintaining combustion air paths, upgrading in-suite appliances to ENERGY STAR models as they fail, and replacing non-programmable thermostats with programmable or smart thermostats. These actions reduce long-term maintenance costs, improve system efficiency and extend equipment life with relatively low capital investment.

measures.existing_conditions: At the present, the building relies on external utilities to provide electricity to power the building which might lead to high electrical energy costs.
measures.notes: Install net metered solar PV generated electricity to offset electricity consumption.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
The current state of the solar industry in Ontario is focused on “net metering” as power export to the grid is no longer an option. Rather than power export, net metered solar facilities use the generated electricity to offset electricity consumption within the facility. Since power export is not feasible, the system should be sized to only meet the baseload energy consumption of the building. This building has a high electrical consumption and ample roof space, which makes it a candidate for solar PV. 

A preliminary study is required to accurately estimate the system cost and savings for a Solar PV system

Loss of insulating gas or degradation of the sealed air space between panes can reduce overall thermal performance. While the existing windows were observed to be in generally fair condition, it would be prudent to incorporate sealant renewal and eventual glazing upgrades into the building’s long-term capital planning strategy.

misc_items.text: Lighting throughout the building is generally in good working order. Common areas, corridors, and service spaces appear to be equipped with a mix of LED and fluorescent fixtures. No widespread outages were observed during the walkthrough, and the overall lighting levels were appropriate for the building’s use. Further savings may be available through continued LED retrofit and the use of occupancy-based controls in selected low-traffic areas. Or installing light control in the parking area.
misc_items.title: Lighting condition and controls

While the panel appeared to be functional and no immediate safety deficiencies were observed during the site visit, its configuration and capacity reflect outdated electrical standards and may offer limited flexibility to support future electrical loads, energy-efficiency upgrades, or electrification initiatives. Further detailed electrical assessment is recommended prior to implementing major electrical or energy-related retrofits to confirm available capacity, code compliance, and long-term suitability

misc_items.title: No Insuite Thermostat

misc_items.text: General maintenance observations include isolated leakage at mechanical fittings and signs of aging insulation in select areas. Continued preventive maintenance and timely repair of minor leaks will help preserve system performance and avoid escalation into larger service issues.
misc_items.title: Leakage and maintenance notes

misc_items.text: Additional BAS-related observations include minor gaps in trend logging and limited visibility into select end-use loads. Integrating remaining standalone controllers into the BAS would improve reporting, enable more consistent scheduling, and simplify ongoing monitoring.
